passages.t: ‘I am in favor of peace’: the first Song of Ascents
passages.happening:
The heading is new: “A song of ascents” (verse 1). The prayer is short. “In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me” (verse 1). “Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips and a deceitful tongue” (verse 2).

The singer turns and speaks to the liar. What will God do to you, “O deceitful tongue?” (verse 3). The answer: “Sharp arrows will come from the warrior, with burning coals of the broom tree!” (verse 4).

Then he groans about where he lives. “Woe to me that I dwell in Meshech, that I live among the tents of Kedar!” (verse 5). “Too long have I dwelt among those who hate peace” (verse 6). The psalm ends with no answer to the trouble. “I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 120 begins a group of fifteen psalms, 120 to 134, each headed ‘A song of ascents’. What the heading means is not certain, and this note explains it once for all fifteen.

The most common view is that these were songs for pilgrims. The law called Israel's men to come before the LORD three times a year, at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 16:16). Jerusalem sits high in the hills of Judah, so people always spoke of going ‘up’ to it. Luke tells how Jesus' family “went up according to the custom of the Feast” when he was twelve (Luke 2:42). On this reading, families sang these short psalms as they travelled up to the city, and in its courts.

There are other views. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, says the temple had fifteen steps between two of its courts, matching the fifteen Songs of Ascents, where Levites sang with instruments at the Feast of Tabernacles. It does not say these were the songs they sang there. Some link ‘going up’ with the return from Babylon, since Ezra 7:9 uses the same Hebrew word, ma'alah, for Ezra's trip back from Babylon. The book page calls the pilgrim reading likely, not certain, and so do these notes.

Psalm 120 starts far from Jerusalem. Meshech was a people of the far north (Genesis 10:2), and Kedar a desert tribe of Arabia, named among the sons of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13). They lay hundreds of miles apart, so most readers take them as pictures: living among hostile strangers, far from home. The broom tree was a desert bush whose wood burned very hot. A lying tongue wounds like an arrow and burns like coal, so its punishment fits.
passages.later:
James wrote, “The tongue also is a fire, a world of wickedness among the parts of the body” (James 3:6).

Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). Paul wrote, “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18). Both know, like this psalm, that it is not always possible.
passages.asks:
The pilgrim songs begin in a place of lies and conflict. That is honest. Many people start toward God not because life is calm, but because they are worn out by where they are.

Are you living among people who twist your words, or who want war when you want peace? This psalm lets you say so to God. And it is the first step of a longer road. The next psalms go up to Jerusalem.
